name: ABS-ESD (Static-Dissipative ABS)
chemical_makeup: The same amorphous acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene terpolymer as base ABS, compounded with a permanent, non-migratory conductive carbon additive. The additive chemistry differs by brand and is the main reason the electrical numbers do: 3DXTech's 3DXSTAT ESD-ABS uses multi-wall carbon nanotubes in a premium ABS base, while eSUN describes an 'antistatic modified ABS' reaching surface resistance as low as 10⁵ Ω without naming the filler (carbon black is the usual choice for that band, but eSUN does not say so — unverified). Loading is low compared with a structural composite: enough to build a conductive network, not enough to reinforce. Always black, because the filler is.
summary: Base ABS made static-dissipative for electronics work, and the tougher, hotter-running counterpart to petg-esd. Deltas vs abs: surface resistance controlled down to about 10⁵ Ω, tensile down slightly to 38 MPa XY, a pronounced Z penalty (22 MPa Z tensile and only 2.1 kJ/m² Z impact against 19.29 kJ/m² XY), density oddly low at 0.97 g/cm³, and a specialist price. Almost nothing else moves — HDT 96 °C against base ABS's 99 °C, same enclosure need, same styrene emissions, and notably no hardened-nozzle requirement, which is the clearest delta against abs-cf. Deltas vs petg-esd: three to four orders of magnitude more dissipative (10⁵ Ω against 10⁹ Ω) and 28 °C more heat resistance, but a warp-prone styrenic process instead of an easy copolyester one.

printing.notes: Brand spread is wide in the same pattern as abs-cf: eSUN 250-280 °C nozzle / 70-90 °C bed, 3DXTech 3DXSTAT ESD-ABS 220-240 °C / 100-110 °C — the recorded window is a union of two non-overlapping recommendations, so read the spool's datasheet. Bed follows the higher figures because base ABS behaviour dominates once the part is on the plate. The one genuinely permissive delta against every filled grade in this cluster is the nozzle: neither vendor flags this material as abrasive, because a low-loading conductive carbon or nanotube additive is nothing like chopped fiber, so a standard brass nozzle should serve (no explicit vendor statement either way — unverified, and a hardened nozzle costs nothing to fit if in doubt). eSUN allows 10-40 % part cooling, unusual for an ABS-family material and more generous than base ABS's 0-20 %, and rates the material to 300 mm/s. 3DXTech recommends a heated chamber; eSUN does not state one, and standard ABS practice — sealed, draft-free, passive enclosure — is sufficient for typical parts, so heated_chamber_required stays false as on abs and abs-cf.

feeding.notes: Rigid, so any extruder feeds it; not an elastomer, so no shore hardness and no feeding assistant. Feeding behaviour is essentially base ABS's — this is not a fiber composite, so the brittleness and PTFE-abrasion arguments that bar pa6-cf and pet-cf from a material station do not apply with anything like the same force. Recorded 'conditional' rather than base ABS's plain 'yes' for the same reason petg-esd is: the conductive carbon filler is mildly abrasive over a long PTFE feed path, no vendor documents this grade in a material station (unverified), and conductive dust in a feed path is an unquantified nuisance around electronics. Standard brass or steel drive gears are sufficient.

drying.dryness_validation: No popping, crackling or steam at the nozzle and no bubbles in a purge strand. Gloss is a weak indicator here because the carbon-loaded surface is dark and flat, the same caveat recorded on petg-esd — judge by sound and strand quality.
drying.notes: eSUN specifies 70 °C for over 8 h and 3DXTech 80 °C for 4 h — identical to the same two brands' ABS-CF schedules and inside base ABS's 70-85 °C / 4-8 h band. The ESD additive changes hygroscopy not at all, so this stays a store-it-sealed material rather than a dry-before-every-print one, unlike pa-cf.

storage.recommendations: Sealed box or drybox with desiccant between prints, as for base ABS. Moisture behaviour is the base material's; the only reason to be stricter is the price of the filament, not its chemistry.

price.notes: The weakest data in this entry. Neither eSUN's nor 3DXTech's ESD-ABS listing yielded a price during research (unverified), so the band is bracketed by analogy: eSUN's specialty grades and the wider ESD filament market anchor a $45-55/kg low end, while 3DXTech's own ESD line prices its ESD-PETG at $105-140/kg and its ESD-ABS should be expected in that tier. Treat the range as indicative only, and note that it spans the same budget-versus-premium split visible in abs-cf's $32-70/kg.

recommended: ESD-safe jigs, fixtures and trays for PCB and IC handling
enclosures and casings for electrostatic-sensitive devices
robot and automation components carrying sensitive electronics
static-dissipative guards and covers on production lines
ESD-safe tooling that also needs to hold shape near 90 °C, where petg-esd (HDT 68-76 °C) gives up
replacing machined ESD plastics for low-volume fixtures
not_recommended: any part needing a colour other than black
outdoor or UV-exposed service — the ESD additive does nothing for ABS's polybutadiene UV weakness
parts loaded in Z: Z impact strength is 2.1 kJ/m² against 19.29 kJ/m² XY, the widest anisotropy gap in this cluster
stiff structural parts — use abs-cf, which reinforces where this additive only conducts
printing in an unventilated occupied room (styrene fumes)
cost-sensitive work where plain ABS would do

properties.notes: eSUN ABS-ESD: density 0.97 g/cm³, surface resistance as low as 10⁵ Ω (permanent, non-migratory), tensile 38 MPa XY / 22 MPa Z, flexural 63 MPa XY / 35.9 MPa Z, elongation at break 4.8 % XY / 3.1 % Z, Charpy impact 19.29 kJ/m² XY / 2.1 kJ/m² Z, HDT@0.45 MPa 96 °C. Two figures deserve attention. The density is the odd one: 0.97 g/cm³ is BELOW base ABS's 1.05 and below every filled grade here, which is the opposite of what adding carbon should do — it is recorded as published but should be re-verified, and if correct it makes this the highest part-volume-per-spool material in the styrenic family at 103.1 cm³ per 100 g. The Z impact figure is the other: a 9:1 XY-to-Z ratio is far worse than abs-cf's 0.69 tensile ratio or petg-esd's 0.40, suggesting the conductive network concentrates at layer interfaces (mechanism inferred from the data pattern, unverified). Mechanically the additive is functional, not structural: 38 MPa tensile sits inside base ABS's own 30-45 MPa band and below abs-cf's 43.3 MPa, and HDT 96 °C is fractionally under base ABS's 99 °C. Tg and max service temperature are carried from the base abs entry; shrinkage is unpublished and omitted. For calibration, the sibling petg-esd runs 10⁹ Ω surface resistivity and 68-76 °C HDT — this grade is three to four orders of magnitude more dissipative and 20-28 °C more heat-resistant.

compatibility.notes: Welds to itself and across the styrenic family on the shared SAN matrix — the useful case being an ESD-safe contact surface printed onto an otherwise plain ABS fixture, spending the expensive filament only where charge control matters, exactly as recorded for petg-esd on plain PETG (mechanical soundness inferred from shared chemistry, unverified — and note that a multi-material ESD part is only dissipative where the ESD material actually is). HIPS is the family's breakaway and D-limonene-soluble support, documented for base ABS and inferred here; a conductive additive could in principle affect the solvent-support interaction, which no source tests (unverified). PLA, PETG, PVA and BVOH are all out on temperature. Not listed as a support for other materials — far too expensive for the role.

plate_recommendations.notes: Textured PEI at 90-110 °C with an adhesion aid, following base ABS practice — the ESD additive does nothing for warp, so the glue stick or ABS promoter plus a brim matters more here than on abs-cf, where the fiber helps. Not vendor-documented for ESD grades (unverified).
Workable with glue, as for base ABS; textured is the safer choice given full base-ABS corner-lift force.
As base ABS: workable with an adhesion aid, but a rigid plate gives a warping styrenic nothing to yield against, so brim generously.
As base ABS: the coating is not rated for the bed temperatures this material wants.
Same thermal exclusion as base ABS.
As base ABS: a polyolefin coating does not hold a styrenic.

alternatives.reason: The easy-process ESD option: open-frame, far less warp (3 vs 8) and easier overall (ease 6 vs 4) — but three to four orders of magnitude less dissipative (10⁹ Ω vs 10⁵ Ω) and ~28 °C less heat resistance (temp 5 vs 7).
Plain ABS at a fraction of the cost ($18-35 vs $45-140) with better compression (7 vs 6) and layer adhesion (5 vs 4), if the part does not actually need a controlled surface resistance.

Same base with a large stiffness and warp gain instead of an electrical spec (dim 8 vs 4, warp 5 vs 8, adhesion 5 vs 4) at lower cost ($32-70 vs $45-140) — but its conductivity is unspecified and uncontrolled, and it requires a hardened nozzle where ABS-ESD does not.

If heat and stiffness matter more than the resistance spec, PC-ABS is cheaper ($44-48 vs $45-140), stronger (compression 7 vs 6) and better-bonded (adhesion 7 vs 4) in an ABS-like process — with no ESD control.

emissions.notes: Base ABS's emission profile unchanged — styrene plus ultrafine-particle rates roughly 100-1000x PLA's (Azimi et al., ES&T) — which puts this in the worst tier alongside abs-cf, abs-gf and asa-cf, and far above sibling petg-esd's low-VOC copolyester profile. Whether carbon nanotube or carbon black additives contribute their own emissions during printing is unstudied (unverified). Print in a vented enclosure or filter through HEPA plus activated carbon. The bench hazard is distinct: sanding or drilling liberates fine conductive dust, which is both a respiratory irritant and a short-circuit risk around energised electronics — precisely the environment this material is bought for.

safety_notes: Styrene is a respiratory irritant and a suspected carcinogen with chronic exposure; ventilation is not optional. Do not sand or machine parts without respiratory protection and dust capture — the filler fines are conductive, so keep them away from live electronics and clean the bench afterwards. Not food-contact suitable: the conductive additive rules it out regardless of anything else. Do not treat a printed part as a verified ESD control item without measuring it — as documented on petg-esd, printed surface resistivity moves with print temperature, and the two brands here target bands three to four orders of magnitude apart. No hardened nozzle is required, unlike every fiber-filled grade in this cluster.
additional_notes: Choose between the two ESD entries on temperature and on how dissipative the part must be, not on price. ABS-ESD reaches about 10⁵ Ω against petg-esd's 10⁹ Ω — the difference between conductive-tier and the upper edge of the dissipative band, which for some workplace ESD standards decides the material outright — and holds 96 °C HDT against 68-76 °C. What it gives up is the easy print: this is full base-ABS warp behaviour with a styrene emission profile, where petg-esd prints on an open frame. Verify resistivity on your own coupons rather than trusting the spool label, and design against Z loading deliberately: a 9:1 XY-to-Z impact ratio means an ESD tray that survives being dropped flat may shatter dropped on edge. Against abs-cf, the split is clean: the fiber grade reinforces and needs a hardened nozzle, this one conducts and does not.

provenance.conflicts: Additive chemistry differs by brand and is disclosed by only one: 3DXTech names multi-wall carbon nanotubes, eSUN says only 'antistatic modified ABS' — so the entry describes a functional class, not one compound. Nozzle and bed temperatures do not overlap between the two brands (eSUN 250-280 °C / 70-90 °C, 3DXTech 220-240 °C / 100-110 °C), the same unexplained pattern seen on abs-cf. Density 0.97 g/cm³ is a single eSUN figure and is anomalous — below unfilled ABS, which adding carbon should not produce — and needs re-verification. Pricing could not be established for either brand and the recorded band is bracketed by analogy to the wider ESD filament market and to 3DXTech's ESD-PETG pricing; treat it as an estimate. Surface resistance is quoted as 'as low as 10⁵ Ω' by eSUN with no band and no method, and 3DXTech publishes no figure on the fetched page, so the material has no single electrical specification — and petg-esd's sourced data shows printed resistivity moving two orders of magnitude with a 20 °C nozzle change, which almost certainly applies here too (unverified for this grade). Hardened-nozzle status is recorded false because neither vendor flags abrasion, not because either states it is unnecessary. Tg, max service temperature and plate ratings are carried from base ABS; shrinkage is unpublished and omitted. HIPS support pairing is inherited from ABS chemistry and untested against a conductive additive. The layer-interface explanation for the 9:1 Z impact ratio is inferred from the data pattern alone.
